chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Yahya ibn Abi Imran al-Hamdani, who said:

I wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), 'May I be sacrificed for you! What do you say regarding a man who begins with 'In the Name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful' in his prayer, alone in the Mother of the Book (Surah Al-Fatiha). So when he comes to other than the Mother of the Book from the Surah, he leaves it.' So the Abbasid said, 'There is no problem with that.' So he (peace be upon him) wrote by his own handwriting: 'Repeat it twice, notwithstanding his nose,' meaning the Abbasid.

key_terms.أُمِّ الْكِتَابِ: The Mother of the Book (Surah Al-Fatiha)
key_terms.الْعَبَّاسِيُّ: The Abbasid (referring to Caliph al-Mansur or his era)
key_terms.بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ: In the Name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful (Basmalah)
key_terms.عَلَى رَغْمِ أَنْفِهِ: Noto his nose / Despite his pride

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on reciting the Basmalah in every Surah during individual prayer according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the jurisprudential debate regarding the recitation of the *Basmalah* at the start of each Surah during prayer, specifically contrasting the view of the Abbasid Caliph with that of Imam al-Sadiq (AS). The Imam’s written response, instructing the repetition of the *Basmalah* 'to his nose' (a phrase indicating emphatic insistence or slight disdain for the opposing view), underscores the Shia emphasis on the ritual completeness of Quranic recitation in Salah. This ruling highlights the distinct scholarly tradition of treating the *Basmalah* as an integral verse of every Surah, thereby affecting the structure and validity of individual prayer recitations.
